parties:
Nasir Ahmed
Vs.
Bangladesh and others
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain, J: This Rule was issued on an application for revision made by the plaintiff under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure (the Code) against judgment and decree dated 30.4.1992 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Bhola in Title Appeal No. 54 of 1987 affirming judgment and decree dated 29.4.1987 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Bhola in Title Suit No.186 of 1982 dismissing the suit.

2. The plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of title by adverse possession and also for permanent injunction. Subsequently, the plaintiff amended the prayer and prayed for recovery of khas possession.

3. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that on getting possession in the shop of plot No. 1110 from the then possessor Rafizal Hoque Bepari he started grocery shop on 10.1.1964. Subsequently, while running the business of books in the name of Al-Amin Library, he entered into a contract to purchase the suit properties including the huts and building thereon with Advocate Birendra Nath Sen Gupta, a lawyer of Bhola Bar Association, the constituted Attorney of Chuni Lal Sen Gupta and others, the original owners of the suit properties. The Attorney received Tk.4,000/- on 15.5.1967 as an advance out of the total consideration of Tk.50,000/- and executed an agreement in favour of the plaintiff. As the plaintiff was given delivery of possession of the suit properties he was not worried because of the delay caused for various reasons in execution and registration of the deed of sale. Moreover, the plaintiff has been living there with his family and carrying on business in the suit properties for more than 12 years by paying municipal taxes. The then S.D.O. and CO. (Rev), Bhola claimed the suit properties in Miscellaneous Case No. 2(S.A.)/63-64 under section 92(a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The constituted Attorney of the original owners filed Title Suit No.496 of 1963 renumbered as Title Suit No. 54 of 1988 in the 1st Court of the then Munsif, Bhola, which was decreed on 30.12.1978 declaring all the proceedings of the Miscellaneous Case as illegal and without jurisdiction. When defendant No. 1 tried to lease out the suit properties claiming the same as khas the plaintiff filed a petition for taking lease of the same just to avoid the imminent threat of being evicted. He filed Title Suit No. 358 of 1976 for permanent injunction and obtained an ad-interim order of injunction. When the said order of injunction was vacated, the plaintiff preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 169 of 1976 and obtained an order of stay. When the said Miscellaneous Appeal was dismissed on 31.8.1981, the defendants conspired to evict the plaintiff from the suit properties and as such, the plaintiff was constrained to file the instant suit.

4. Defendant No. 3 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint. His case, in short, is that the suit is not maintainable as framed. The suit is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. It is barred by limitation. It is bad for defect of parties. The further case of this defendant is that Chuni Lal Sen and others, the original owners of the suit properties, left for India in 1950 without disposing of the suit properties as a result of which there was none to pay the rent of the same. As such, the suit properties were sold in auction on account of non-payment of rent. In auction, the suit properties were sold to defendant No. 1 on 30.10.1963 and sale was duly confirmed on 30.12.1963. Accordingly, the suit properties became the khash land of khatian No. 1 of the government. Subsequently, suit plot Nos. 1109, 1115, 1111 were leased out to different persons in Settlement Case No. 142 BH/63-64 and those lessees had been possessing the same. Masuma Khatoon Girls' High School has been running in suit plot No. 1102 contiguous to suit plot No. 1103. This defendant got settlement of the entire land of suit plot No.1103 in two instalments. Defendant No. 3 constructed a semi pucca but on the leased land and had since been in possession thereof. The plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 358 of 1976 in the Court of Munsif for permanent injunction in respect of the suit properties but the suit was dismissed on 11.8.1984. There are one temple and a building in the suit plot No. 1103 and Nanibala Datta had been living in that building as a licensee under the original owner. When she left the building during the War of Liberation in 1971, the plaintiff illegally entered into the building by breaking open the lock and continued his illegal possession in the building of suit plot No.1103. To legalise his unlawful possession, the plaintiff collusively created an antedated agreement claiming the suit properties by forging the signature of deceased Birendra Nath Sen Gupta who left the country for India before 15.5.67 and died there. On 28.6.1982, the plaintiff was evicted from his unlawful possession of the suit properties. The plaintiff filed a petition for getting lease of the suit properties before the appropriate authority on different occasions admitting the suit properties to be the khas land of the government. Title Appeal No. 15 of 1979 preferred by the government was allowed on contest setting aside the decree passed in favour of the plain-tiff in Title Suit No. 54 of 1968. Subsequently, the defendant was given lease of the entire land of suit plot No. 1103 permanently. For the reasons stated, the suit of the plaintiff is liable to be dismissed with costs.

5. Both the parties examined witnesses and exhibited documents in support of their respective cases.

6. The trial Court dismissed the suit. On an appeal therefrom at the instance of the plaintiff, the Court of appeal below dismissed the appeal, affirming judgment and decree passed by the trial Court.

7. Being aggrieved by, and dissatisfied with, impugned judgment and decree, the plaintiff as petitioner obtained this Rule from this Court.

8. Mr. Md. Khurshid Alam Khan, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits (1) that both the Courts below found that the suit was bad for defect of parties although a suit should not be dismissed for defect of parties and that the plaintiff should have been given a chance to rectify the defect, (2) that the plaintiff entered into the suit land on the basis of a bainapatra which was executed by the Attorney of the admitted owners and that after passage of statutory period of limitation. the plaintiff acquired title in the suit land by adverse possession, (3) that the plaintiff had been able to prove his exclusive possession in the suit land for more than 12 years and as such, he is entitled to the declaration as prayed and (4) that the plaintiff was evicted from the suit land during pendency of the suit and as such, he prayed for recovery of possession.

9. Mr. Farid Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing for opposite party No. 3, on the other hand, supports impugned judgment and decree. He submits that both the Courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff could not prove his title and possession in the suit land and as such, dismissed the suit and therefore, no interference is called for by this Court sitting in revision as there was no failure of justice.

10. Perused the judgments of the Courts below and the record. From the evidence of P.W. 1, it appears that he admitted in cross examination that Abdur Rashid, Abdul Kalam and Jalal Ahmed had been in possession of the suit land. The suit is one for declaration of title by adverse possession but those persons were not impleaded as parties in the suit. Both the Courts, therefore, correctly came to a finding that the suit was bad for defect of parties. This finding having been based on evidence on record does not call for interference by this Court. Moreover there is no scope to give a chance to the plaintiff to rectify the defect as submitted by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioner.

11. The suit land belonged to Chuni Lal Sen Gupta, Amulla Ranjan Sen Gupta and Anil Kumar Sen Gupta. The suit land was sold in auction in Miscellaneous Case No. 2 of 1963-1964. Anil Kumar Sen and the heirs of Chuni Lal Sen and Amulla Ranjan Sen Gupta as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 496 of 1963 renumbered as Title Suit No. 54 of 1968 challenging the auction made in the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case. The suit was decreed as it appeared from the judgment (Exhibit-1) of the suit. The government preferred an appeal against judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 54 of 1968 and the Court of appeal below allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit as it appeared from the judgment (Exhibit-J) passed in the appeal. As such, the original owners had no title in the suit-land after the passing of judgment and decree in the appeal.

12. Moreover, the record reveals that the original owners contested the suit as well as the appeal themselves and not through their Attorney, Advocate Dhirendra Nath Sen Gupta. As such, it is doubtful whether or not Advocate Dhirendra Nath Sen was at all the Attorney of the original owners.

13. Since the auction of the suit land was found valid in Title Appeal No. 15 of 1979, the original owners had no title in the suit land. Therefore, the so called constituted Attorney had no authority to enter into any contract with the plaintiff to sell the suit property on 15.5.1967 The plaintiff filed the judgment passed in Title Suit No. 496 of 1963 renumbered as Title Suit No. 54 of 1968 but suppressed the appeal filed against the decree of the suit. The appeal being Title Appeal No. 15 of 1979 was allowed and the suit was dismissed. As such, the finding of the Courts below that the plaintiff failed to prove his contract dated 15.5.1967 is based on evidence on record. The judgments of the Courts below reveal that the plaintiff filed an application for taking lease of the suit properties from the government as evident from the record of Miscellaneous Case No. 1-S.A/B 1981-1982, Case No. 2/1982-1983 and Misc. Case No. 8 B.H/1982-1983. Therefore, the Courts below were justified in holding that the plaintiff was stopped by the principle of estoppel to claim the suit properties by way of adverse possession or otherwise.

<u>14. Both the Courts below concurrently found that the plaintiffs could not prove his possession in the suit land. This finding of the Courts below is also based on evidence of P.Ws. and of D.Ws. It is to be noted here that to believe or to disbelieve a witness is within the jurisdiction of the Courts below and this Court sitting in revision cannot interfere in such jurisdiction unless it can be shown that there is misreading or non-reading of material evidence affecting the ultimate decision of the Courts below. The learned Advocate for the petitioner, however, could not show any misreading or non-reading of evidence.</u>

15. When the case was posted for hearing in the list of this Court the plaintiff and opposite party No. 3 filed an application for compromise. On perusal of the compromise, I find that it is not in form. Moreover, the compromise was written on stamp papers wherein the plaintiff relinquished his claim in respect of the suit plot No. 1103 in favour of the school, defendant No. 3. The application for compromise having been not in form cannot be considered and as such, it is rejected.

16. The reasonings arrived at and the decision made by the Courts below do not suffer any patent illegality or flagrant error of law warranting interference by this Court exercising power under section 115(1) of the Code.

17. For the reasons stated, I do not find any substance in this Rule.

18. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

Send down the Lower Court Record at once.

End.

Motahera Begum and others
Vs.
Abdul Monaf and others
full_judgment:
Syed Abu Kowser Md. Dabirush-Shan, J: This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties No.I-5 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 2.11.2002 and 9.11.2002 respectively passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Cox's Bazar in Other Appeal No.29 of 1999 allowing the appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 28.1.1999 and 31.1.1999 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Cox's Bazar in Other Suit No.45 of 1995 in decreeing the suit should not be set aside.

2. The petitioner being plaintiffs instituted Other Suit No.45 of 1995 in the Court of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Cox's Bazar praying a decree for declaration of title to the land measuring an area of 1.50 acres appertaining to R. S. Khatian No.105, M. R. R. Khatian No.1, Plot No.106, Jomabondi Khatian No.157, Plot No.106 corresponding to B.S. Khatian No.7, Plot No.110, R. S. Khatian No.117, M. R. R. Khatian No.1, Plot No.110 of Mouza-Kaligonj, Police Station-Moheshkhali, District-Cox's Bazar stating in a nut shell that the suit jote belonged to Zaminder Khirod Chandra Roy and others under whom Sahar Ali, Asad Ali Mia were the rioty tenants. The R. S. Khatian was prepared in their names finally Sahar Ali and others being unable to pay rent surrendered khas possession of the said land in favour of Zaminder. The Zaminder took the land in khas possession and settled a portion of the land in favour of the predecessor of the defendant Nos.1-4, the predecessor of the defendant Nos.12,13-21, the defendant No.22 and in favour of the defendant No. 5. Thereafter settled the rest land i.e. the land of Schedule-3 land to the plaint remained as khas land which was vested to the Government by due operation of law. During S.A. operation the said land was recorded in R. S. Plot No.106 an area of 1.39 acres and in R.S. Plot No.110 an area of 11 decimals in R.S. Khatian No. 1. The plaintiff's predecessor was a sailor and that he had no land and property of his own. During the liberation war he was in West Pakistan and he was in service and after liberation of Bangladesh he came to Bangladesh. Since the predecessor of the plaintiffs have no land they improved the land of Schedule-3 and make it cultivable and used to cultivate the land. Thereafter the Government of Bangladesh Vide Settlement Case No.7 of 1973-74 settled the land of Schedule-3 in favour of the predecessor of the plaintiffs without receiving any salami. Subsequently an agreement was executed and registered in between the plaintiff's predecessor and the Government of Bangladesh and the possession of land was hand over to the predecessor of the plaintiffs. Thereafter Jomabondi Case No.157 was open in his name i.e. in the name of Abul Kashem. The Government of Bangladesh handed over the physical possession in favour of Abul Kashem and thereafter the plaintiff's predecessor began to possess the same and have been possessing the suit land till his death and then the plaintiffs have been in possession of the suit land. During the B.S. operation the suit land was not recorded in the name of the plaintiffs and on 28.11.1993, the plaintiffs went to pay the rent to the office of the defendant No.26 who informed him that the B.S. recorded was not prepared in the name of the Government and also in the name of some other defendants and expressed his inability to accept the rent. The suit land is the only land of the plaintiff and that B.S. record having not been prepared in his name the title of the plaintiffs was clouded and hence the plaintiffs were compelled to file the case

3. The defendants No.1-5 contested the suit by filing written statements denying the material allegations made in the plaint and stating, inter alia, that the Zaminder by Patta being No.105 settled the suit land in favour of the defendants predecessor Anu Mia. That thereafter more 10.17 acres of land was settled with Sultan Ahmed and others Vide Patta No.68 of 1976. The M. R. R. Khatian and B. S. Khatian was prepared in their names. The other lands were settled with Sirajul Mostafa and others by Dakhila. The M.R.R. Khatian No.137 was recorded in their names and that the settlement holders have been in possession of 3.82 acres of land in Plot No.106. Hirod Chandra had no subsisting interest in the land of Plot No.106. Thereafter the rent receiving interest was acquired by Zaminder who had no interest and the land was vested to the Government and area of 1.39 acres of land of the defendant was wrongly recorded in khas khatian No. l. That the B. S. Khatian was correctly recorded in respect of 2.51 acres of land and that the Government had no title and possession in the land of Plot No.106 and the Government was not entitled to settle any land from that plot. The Government was not entitled to settle any land from that plot and with these averments the defendants claimed for dismissal of the suit.

4. During the course of trial the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Cox's Bazar on consideration of the evidence on record and after perusing the papers and documents passed the decree in favour of the plaintiff by his judgment and decree dated 28.1.1999 and 31.1.1999 respectively.

5. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree passed by the learned Senior Assistant, Cox's Bazar, the defendant preferred an appeal before the learned District Judge, Cox's Bazar being Other Appeal No.29 of 1999 which was ultimately heard and disposed of by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Cox's Bazar who was pleased to allow the appeal and reverse the judgment and decree passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Cox's Bazar by his judgment and decree dated 2.11.2002 and 9.11.2002 respectively.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Cox's Bazar, the plaintiff-respondent-petitioners preferred the instant revisional application before the High Court Division under Section-115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present rule.

7. The learned Counsel Mr. Golam Rabbani with Mr. Ruhul Bari Sharif appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent-petitioners submits that the learned Joint District, Cox's Bazar is absolutely wrong and erroneous in allowing the appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Cox's Bazar. The learned Counsel next submits that the trial court after scrutinizing and weighing the evidence on record and also perusing the papers and documents passed the judgment and decree which was absolutely correct and proper. The learned trial court rightly observed in his judgment that the Pattas did not specified the suit land as such the suit land is vague and unspecified. The learned Counsel further submits that the defendants ought to have been filed a case for correction of M.R.R.  record if at all the suit land was wrongly recorded in M.R.R. Khatian but the defendant did not take any steps to correct the M. R. R. Khatian. The learned Counsel also submits that the appellate court should reverse the finding of the trial court with reference to the evidence on record but in the instant suit the learned Joint District Judge without referring the evidence on record reverse the finding of the trial court which is absolutely wrong and illegal and as such liable to be interfered by this court. The learned Counsel finally submits that the lower appellate court without taking into consideration of the legal provision of Order-XLI, Rule-31 came to wrong and erroneous finding and acted illegally in reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial court which is liable to be set aside and interfered by this court and hence the rule should be made absolute.

8. On the other hand the learned Counsel Mr. Md. Alamgir Kitbir appearing on behalf of the defendant-appellant-opposite parties submits that the finding of facts whether concurrent or not arrived at by the lower appellate court is final unless it is manifestly perverse. Next he submits that the lower appellate court was absolutely right and justified in arriving at its finding and decision in reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial court because there is no misreading and non-consideration of the evidence on record which calls for no interference by this court in revisional jurisdiction. The learned Counsel further submits that the defendant after obtaining Patta from Zaminder has been owning and possessing the suit land since a long without any interruption from any quarter. He also submits that the argument advance by the learned Counsel for the petitioner that the Patta was unspecified was not correct. The Zaminder by these Pattas distributed all his khas land to different tenant and no khas land was left with the possession of the Zaminder. The learned Counsel further submits that the learned appellate court rightly observed in his judgment that if the Government would acquire the khas land of Zaminder in that case the lessee plaintiff-petitioners would produce compensation assessment roll to prove their bonafide but in the present case the plaintiff-petitioner could not produce any compensation assessment roll to show that Government acquire the suit land from the Zaminder by giving compensation. The learned Counsel to refute the argument of the lawyer of the other side submitted that with regard to preparation of record of right and correct of M.R.R. Khatian he submits that under Section 144 A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act new record will prevail upon the old record. The learned Counsel in support of his contention referred the case of Fatema Khatun -Versus-Faizal Mia reported in 21 B.L.D.(H.C) 14 where in it has been held that:-

"In the event of a conflict between the old Record of right and the recent record of right, recent record of right would prevail in as much as presumption of the record of right loses its weight with the passage of time and entry in the subsequent khatian."

9. The learned Counsel finally submits that the lower appellate court is absolutely right and justified in allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial court. The appellate court did not commit any error of law and there is no infirmity of law which is not liable for any interference by this court and as such the rule should be discharged.

<u>10. On a meticulous examination of the judgment and decree passed by the lower appellate court as well as the trial court and the evidence on record and also the documents and exhibits it transpires that the lower appellate court carefully and clearly discussed the evidence on record and the main point of dispute with regard to the record of right and applying his judicial mind after proper assessment of the evidence on record came to his finding in reversing the judgment and decree passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Cox's Bazar. The learned lower appellate court in its judgment discussed that the plaintiff could not produce the compensation assessment roll to prove that the Government acquire the land from Zaminder after giving proper compensation to the Zaminder. The plaintiff could not prove his case successfully. The learned trial court without applying his judicial mind and without proper assessment of the evidence on record came to wrong and erroneous finding in decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiff. The trial court ought to have been considered that if the Government would acquire the land in that case Government would give proper compensation to the Zaminder after preparing compensation assessment roll and for this reason the Government did not contest the suit. Therefore the lower appellate court is absolutely right and justified in allowing the appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial court and hence no interference is called for by this court.</u>

11. By now the settled principle of law in exercising the revisional power under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been laid down in the several judicial pronouncement of our Appellate Division that the finding of facts whether concurrent or not arrived at by the appellate Court is final unless it is manifestly perverse. In this connection I like to rely on the decision in the case of Khurshid Ali and others -Vs- Noorjahan Bewa and others reported in 15 B.L.D.(A.D) 82 wherein it has been held that:

"When the appellate Court as the final Court of fact decides questions of fact and records its findings on consideration of the evidence on record, the High Court Division while exercising revisional jurisdiction cannot interfere with findings of facts unless the High Court Division is satisfied that the said findings are perverse. When the material findings of the appellate Court are upheld by the High Court Division and in doing so it commits no error of law, the decision of the High Court Division calls for no interference by the Appellate Division".

12. Another Decision can also be cited in the case of Hazari Bala Sana and another -Vs-Niron alias Nironjan Mondal and others reported in 17 B.L.D.(A.D)295 wherein it has been stated that:

"It is a settled principle that the finding of facts whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the lower appellate Court, which is the final Court of fact, is binding on the High Court Division, as a revisional Court except in certain well-defined exceptional circumstances, such as non-consideration or misreading of the material evidence affecting the merit of the case".

13. The judgment of the lower appellate Court transpires that in arriving at its finding the said Court carefully considered all the material facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record both oral and documentary and registered deed affecting the merit of the case. The learned Counsel for the plaintiff-respondent-petitioner could not also point out any error or illegality or infirmity of law in the judgment passed by the lower appellate Court.

14. In view of the discussion made above and the facts and circumstances of the case the impugned judgment and decree dated 2.11.2002 and 9.11.2002 respectively passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Cox's Bazar in Other Appeal No.29 of 1999 allowing the appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 28.1.1999 and 31.1.1999 respectively passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Cox's Bazar in Other Suit No.45 of 1995 and the case having been concluded on finding of facts as such no interference is called for in revision under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

15. In the result, the rule is discharged without and order as to the costs.

16. Lower Courts record be sent down at once with a copy of the judgment.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Babul Kumar Biswas, Advocate ------ For the appellant. 
No-one: For Respondents
parties:
Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation (BHBFC).
Vs.
Rupali Bank Limited and others
full_judgment:
Md. Nuruzzaman, J: This First Miscellaneous appeal, at the instance of creditor Bangladesh House building finance corporation (hereinafter to be called as corporation) is directed against the judgment and order dated 21.10.2008 passed by learned District Judge and Bankruptcy court, Dhaka in Bankruptcy suit No. 01 of 2008 allowing the application filed by auction purchaser under section 110/111 of the Bankruptcy Act setting aside the order dated 11.9.2006 passed by learned Additional District Judge and Bankruptcy court, Dhaka accepting the Draft sale deed of the auction purchaser.

2. Material facts are that creditor Rupali Bank Limited filed the Bankruptcy suit Nos. 7 of 2001 against Messers Zahed Garments, Bankruptcy suit No. 8 of 2001 against Rupam Garments and Bankruptcy suit no. 9 against Zabed Garments for declaration that they are Bankrupt. Bankruptcy suit Nos. 7, 8, 9 of 2001 were decreed on 22.3.2004 25.7.2005 and 23.3.2004 respectively. Thereafter Additional District Judge and Bankruptcy court, Dhaka appointed Acnabin & Co. a chartered Accountants firm as receiver. Receiver published auction notices in Daily Inkilab, Daily Itafaq Daily Observer and Daily Independent on 27th and 28th December 2005 respectively fixing on 07.02.2006 for submitting the quotation. Receiver scrutinized the submitted quotation and accepted the highest bid. Mr. Md. Baker Hossain was the highest bidder. Receiver prepared a draft sale deed and submitted before the court for its approval.

3. Creditor Corporation filed an application under section 83 of the Bankruptcy Act 1997 in the court of Additional District Judge and Bankruptcy court for rejecting the Draft deed of sale submitted by receiver on 23.8.2006 alleging that in Bankruptcy suit Nos. 07,08, and 09 of 2001 Mr. Mohd. Zahed, Mohd Aslam and Mohd. Zabed respectively have been declared as Bankrupt but draft; deed of sale included the property of another brother Mohd. Mahbub against whom Bank did not file any suit, neither has any claim nor he was declared as Bankrupt. It is further alleged that receiver published the notice of auction fixing the last date for submitting of quotation on 07.02.2006 but he received quotation and bank pay order dated 09.05.2006 of Md. Baker Hossain thereby receiver himself committed material fraud on the quotation process and upon the court. It further alleged that though a 4 storied building is standing on the mortgage land but receiver without showing it in the auction notice and draft of sale deed trying to approve the draft deed of sale from the Bankruptcy court. If building has been shown upon the land the price of the property could have been much higher than the quoted price. The creditor corporation earlier informed the receiver that the borrowers earlier took loan mortgaging the suit property to the corporation and constructed building thereon, therefore no charge has been created by the creditor Bank and as such the receiver on behalf of bank has no legal right to auction the property in question because creditor corporation has already got decree from the court of District Judge in Miscellaneous cases filed under P.O. No. 7 of 1973 and execution case is at the stage of auction but the receiver without informing the above facts to the court published the auction notice and took the subsequent steps by practicing fraud upon the court thereby the draft deed of sale dated 23.8.2006 is liable to be rejected. The learned Additional District Judge and Bankruptcy court heard the application and by his order dated 11.9.2007 rejected the draft deed of sale dated 23.8.2006 and directed the receiver to return the deposited money of the auction purchaser. Auction purchaser was directed to withdraw his money with Advance tax and poundage. The learned Additional District Judge and Bankruptcy court's order dated 11.9.2007 though appeal able to the High court Division of Supreme Court but auction purchaser without filing appeal after transferring the cases from the court of Additional District Judge and Bankruptcy court to the court of district Judge, filed an application before the learned District Judge and Bankruptcy court under section 110 and 1 l 1 of the said Act for correction the order dated 11.9.2007 passed by learned Additional District Judge. Learned District Judge and Bankruptcy Court heard the application and by his order dated 21.10.2008 set aside the order dated 11.9.2006 passed by the Additional District Judge and Bankruptcy court.

4. Feeling aggrieved by the order dated 21.10.2008 passed by District Judge and Bankruptcy court in Bankruptcy suit no. 1 of 2008 preferred the instant First Miscellaneous appeal before this court.

<u>5. Mr. Babul Kumar Biswas the learned advocate appearing for the appellant submitted that the learned Additional District Judge and Bankruptcy court by order dated 11.9.2006 allowed the creditor corporation's application by sitting aside the auction sale and rejecting the draft deed of sale having found that the fraud practice committed by the bidder in submitting the quotation and receiver also suppressed the aforesaid facts. However auction purchaser without filing appeal before the higher court misleading the learned District Judge obtained the impugned order from him by filing an application under section 110 and 111 of the Bankruptcy Act. The learned District Judge, Dhaka in passing the impugned order acted illegally and beyond its jurisdiction in allowing the application of the auction purchaser by setting aside the order dated 11.09.2006 passed by learned Additional District Judge and Bankruptcy court and as such the impugned order is liable to be set aside. He further submitted that the learned District Judge misread and misconstrued the section 110 and 111 of the Bankruptcy Act 1997 as such erred in law and facts in passing the impugned order. He added that neither creditor Bank and receiver nor auction purchaser had accrued any legal right in the property in question because earlier property was mortgaged to the corporation thus the Bankrupt persons have no right and authority to mortgage the property to the Creditor Bank without due process of law. He further added that order dated 11.9.06 passed by the learned Additional District Judge and Bankruptcy court cannot set aside its earlier order sitting in same jurisdiction as District Judge and as such the impugned order is liable to be set aside. He lastly submitted that the learned District Judge erred in law in observing that the creditor corporation did not file the application under section 83 of Bankruptcy Act in the court with in the period of limitation because the receiver on 23.8.2006 filed the draft deed of sale in the court and the creditor corporation filed the application on 27.8.2006 which is within the period of limitation.</u>

6. No one appears for the respondents.

7. The points for consideration whether impugned order call for interference by this court.

8. Considering the materials on record it transpires that the appellant calls in question the legality and propriety of the impugned order dated 21.10.2008 passed by the learned District Judge and Bankruptcy court in Bankruptcy suit No. 1 of 2008 setting aside the order dated 11.9.2006 passed by Additional District Judge and Bankruptcy court allowing the application under section 83 of the said Act filed by the appellant as creditor corporation third party for cancelling the draft deed of sale submitted by the receiver. It appears that the receiver on 23.08.2006 filed the draft deed of sale before the court and appellant as third party filed an application under section 83 of the said Act for cancelling the same on the grounds of jurisdiction and fraud.

<u>9. We have gone through the impugned order. It appears from the impugned order that on 21.10.2008 before the learned District Judge two applications were fixed for hearing. One filed by the 3rd party creditor corporation under section 64(4) of the Act read with 53 of the rules framed thereunder for removing the receiver and another filed by the auction purchaser under section 110 and 111 of the said Act for ordering to execute and register the sale deed in favour of him after correcting the order no. 52 dated 11.09.2006. The learned District Judge heard both the application and disposed of by the impugned order rejecting the application for removal of receiver and allowed the application under section 110 and 111 of the said Act cancelling the order no. 52 dated 11.9.2006 accepting the draft deed directing the appeal assistant if possible to final the sale deed and report to that effect within 30.10.2008. From the facts and circumstances of the case and law relevant for disposal the matter we find that crux points in the appeal to consider whether learned District Judge and Bankruptcy court is competent to entertain and hear the application not to correct but to set aside his earlier order which is appealable. Before proceeding to consider the matter we feel it necessary to quote the relevant sections 4, 96,110 and 111 of the said Act for convenient of discussion which runs as follows:</u>

According to sub section (1) of section 4 of the Act the District court is the competent court and District Judge is the Judge who will be competent Judge to hear and dispose of the cases and sub-section (2) of section 4 empowered the District Judge to delegate his power any of the Additional District Judge working within his District to try and dispose the cases which will be treat as Bankruptcy court. According to section 96 of the said Act order passed by Additional District Judge or District Judge is appealable order to the High court Division of the Supreme Court. Section 110 of the Act provides inherent power to resist the abuse of the process of court for the ends of justice wherein section 111 provides power of the court to correct its mistake shows on the face of the record, clerical or arithmetical but not to set aside any order which is appealable. It appears that learned District Judge by its impugned order dated 21.10.2008 allowed the application by setting aside the earlier order dated 11.09.2006 is beyond the ambit of section 110 and 111 of the Act. It is settled principle that court has a wider discretion to apply inherent power to prevent the misuse process of court or to secure ends of justice where there is no specific provision in law to provide any remedy. It is well settled that inherent power of the court should be used judicially and lawfully not fancifully and whimsically. However, in the instant case impugned order dated 11.09.2006 is appealable under section 96 of the Bankruptcy Act. It is an age old axiom principle settled by the apex court of Bangladesh that when an alternative remedy is available to the party court cannot exercise its inherent power. This view lends support from the case of Md. shahidur Rahman Majumder and others Vs. Saberun Nessa and others reported in XVI B.L.D 1996 (AD) 50 where their lordships has held that "when a specific provision for appeal has been provided in the code the court cannot exercise its inherent power under section 151 of the code of civil procedure."</u>

11. Section 110 of the Bankruptcy Act 1997 provides the inherent powers of the court but specifically provided that when there is specific provision for remedy this section would not be applicable for those purposes.

12. So, the grounds urged and contentions advanced by the learned advocate for the appellant have a good deal of force and are the correct exposition of law and facts of the instant appeal. The impugned order of the court below is tainted with legal infirmity and perversity justifies interference by this court.

13. In the light of discussion made above, we find substance in the appeal.

14. Thus, the appeal, having merit succeeds.

15. In the result, the appeal is allowed. The impugned order dated 21.10.2008 passed by learned District Judge, Dhaka in Bankruptcy suit No. 1 of 2008 is hereby set aside.

16. The office is directed to communicate the order at once.

End.

Facts relevant for disposal of the civil revision case are that the petitioner of this revision case instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 65 of 1989 in the Court of learned Sub-ordinate Judge, Naogaon against the opposite parties and that suit was decreed for realisation of Tk.2,30,000/- along with an interest at the rate of Tk.15% upon the principle amount by the judgment and decree dated 5.11.1990. The opposite parties of the rule being defendant preferred First Appeal No. 212 of 1990 before the High Court Division and that appeal was dismissed by the judgment and decree dated 04.12.1995 with some modification of the trial Court's judgment and decree. This Court in dismissing the appeal minimized the principle decretal amount from Tk. 2,30,000/- to Tk.1,62,000/- and assessed compensation @ Tk.10% upon the decretal amount in place of Tk.15%. The petitioner being the decree holder started Other Execution Case No. 3 of 1990 on 24.1.1990 to put the decree into execution. After the disposal of First Appeal No. 212 of 1990 the petitioner amended the application already submitted for execution of the decree and prayed for realisation of Tk.1,62,000/- with 10% interest and that was allowed. The opposite party failed to appear before the Executing Court and as such the Court started proceeding with the Execution Case. The decree holder petitioner ultimately made prayer for attachment of the judgment debtors' property and for realization of decretal amount after selling out the said property in auction and that prayer was allowed. On several occasions, the dates were fixed for selling out property in auction but none turned up to participate the auction purchase. Ultimately the decree holder petitioner submitted an application on 11.9.2000 for allowing him to purchase auction but that application was kept with record. The executing Court again directed the decree holder for publishing proclamation for sale through daily newspapers by order dated 16.10.2000 and thereafter the petitioners on several occasions published the proclamation of auction sale through the daily newspaper but non came forward to purchase. Ultimately the executing Court by order dated 27.10.2002 allowed the application of the petitioners for participating him in the auction and accordingly the petitioner purchased the auction and the petitioners were directed to deposit requisites stamp papers for preparation of sale certificate by order dated 17.5.2003 fixing 26.6.2003 for further order. The petitioners ultimately supplied stamp papers on 29.1.2004 and also submitted a bank draft for Tk.20,447/- and that was accepted by the Court. The sale certificate was written and prepared on 10.4.2004 and that was signed by executing Court vide Order No. 97 and the said sale certificate was sent to the Sub-registrar at Naogaon for registration. The sale certificate was duly registered and thereafter the decree holder submitted an application on 26.4.2004 seeking for getting delivery of possession through Court in the auction purchased land and accordingly the executing Court issued writ of delivery of possession by order dated 26.4.2004 fixing 26.5.2004 for return. The writ of delivery of possession was issued vide order No. 99 dated 26.4.2004. Thereafter the judgment debtors opposite parties entered appearance in the said Execution Proceedings on 15.5.2004 and prayed for staying the proceedings of the Execution Case. At that stage Bangladesh Shipla Bank submitted an application on 17.5.2004 for adding him as a party and that was rejected by order dated 26.5.2004. By that order the application of the judgment debtors were also rejected. The prayer of the petitioner for delivery of possession through police force was allowed fixing 29.6.2004 for further order and thereafter the judgment debtors submitted an application on 12.6.2004 under Order 21 Rule 90 for getting the auction sale set aside and also for staying the execution proceedings. During pendency of the application seeking for getting delivery of possession with the help of police force, the present opposite party submitted an application on 25.4.2005 under section 33(1) of the Bankruptcy Act, 1997 contending, inter alia, that by filing Bankruptcy Case No. 2 of 2003 the opposite party has been declared as bankrupt and as such the execution case is liable to be transferred to the Bankruptcy Court at Dhaka. The learned executing Court allowed the said application by order dated 25.9.2005.

3. Being aggrieved by the said order the petitioners preferred a Civil Revision case being No. 62 of 2005 and that case was heard by the learned Additional District Judge 2nd Court, Naogaon who by the impugned judgment and order dated 18.9.2006 rejected the revision case and affirmed the judgment of the executing Court.

4. Being aggrieved by the impugned order the petitioners decree holders have moved this Court by filing this 2nd revision case. There is no appearance from the part of the opposite party till now. Mr. Mansur Habib, the learned Advocate appearing for the decree holder petitioner took me through the impugned order as well as the order of the executing Court dated 5.9.2005 allowing application made under section 33 (1) of the Act, 1997 and transferring the execution case No. 3 of 1990 to the Bankruptcy Court at Dhaka.

5. Mr. Mansur Habib, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner formulated the following points of arguments:-

(a) the executing Court erred in law in transferring the execution case from his Court to another Court at Dhaka who was not at all concerned with the subject matter of the execution case;

(b) the application of section 33(1) of the Act, 1997 was not at all available in a pending execution case which has arisen out of decree passed in Title Suit and modified by the High Court Division;

(c) the executing Court had to execute the decree as it stands and was not authorised by law to transfer the said execution case to the Bankruptcy Court at Dhaka;

(d) the decree has been partly executed and only a part for getting delivery of possession through Court is required to be executed and at that stage the executing Court was not authorised by law to transfer the case upon receiving application from the judgment debtors. With these submissions he prayed for making the rule absolute and for directing the executing Court to execute the decree as it stand.

6. I have considered the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

7. This Court at the time of issuance of the Rule has called for the record of execution case as well as the record of civil revision case No. 62 of 2005.

8. Upon perusal of the order sheets of Execution Case No. 3 of 1990 as well as the execution application it appears that a title suit was instituted in 1989 and that was decreed on contest. The trial Court allowed a money decree and that decree was appealed before this Court and the judgment debtors were the appellants. This Court minimized the principle amount from Tk.2,30,000/- to Tk1,62,000/- and reduced interest from 15% to 10% and that decree was not challenged by the judgment debtors. The execution case No. 3 of 1990 was started after passing the decree by the trial Court and before disposal of first appeal. After disposal of First Appeal the application for execution was amended and the judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal was made the subject matter of execution proceeding by way of amendment.

9. In view of the above the decree passed by this Court in First Appeal No. 212 of 1990 has been accepted by the judgment debtors. Thereafter decree holders have taken all possible steps for executing the decree, realisation of decretal amount through Court upon selling out the property of the judgment debtors in auction but none came forward to purchase auction and at that stage the decree holder finding no other means to realisation of money had to make a prayer before the executing Court for allowing them to purchase the property in auction and that was ultimately allowed. The judgment debtors were well aware about the pendency of the execution Case No. 3 of 1990 inasmuch as they submitted an application on 29.1.1991 for staying all further proceedings of Execution Case No. 3 of 1990 for the cause of pendency of First Appeal No. 212 of 1990 and at that time the Tender No. was 536 of 1990. Since the judgment of the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 212 of 1990 was passed on 4.12.1995 and the judgment was not called in question by filing Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal that judgment was very much binding upon the judgment debtors opposite parties. From the record of Execution Case No. 3 of 1990 it shows that the property of the opposite party has been purchased by the petitioner in execution of the decree and the sale certificate has been executed and registered which means that the decree has been executed in part.

10. Now the only part has to be executed for handing over possession in the auction purchased land through Court. The decree holder petitioners duly took steps by submitting application for getting possession through Court with the help of police force and that has also been allowed. One police officer and 6 constables were deputed for handing over possession and in the meantime the judgment debtors submitted an application for transferring the case from the Sub-ordinate Judge, Artha Rin Adalat, Naogaon to the Bankruptcy Court at Dhaka for disposal on the ground that the judgment debtor has already been declared as bankrupt vide Case No. 2 of 2003 and that application was allowed. The said order has been affirmed by the Additional District Judge, Naogaon by the impugned order.

11. From the checkered history of the case as discussed aforementioned it shifts a burden upon this Court to decide the following question of law:-

(a) whether the Bankruptcy Act. 1997 is a retrospective legislation?

(b) Whether section 33(1) of the Bankruptcy Act, 1997 has got any manner of application in a partly executed execution proceeding which has been started long before the promulgation of the said Act.

(c) whether the Bankruptcy Court at Dhaka has any jurisdiction to execute the judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 212 of 1990;

(d) whether the Sub-ordinate Judge, Naogaon being the executing Court had any jurisdiction to allow application under section 33(1) of the Bankruptcy Act, 1997 in a pending case and

(e) whether the impugned judgment and order passed by the learned Additional District Judge is lawful.

Let us take up all the above questions together for answer.

12. To answer all these questions let us go through the Bankruptcy Act, 1997. On perusal of said Act it appears that the purpose of promulgation of said Act was only for easy disposal of loan cases between financial institution granting loan and the loanee. After promulgation of Insolvency Act 1997 the Insolvency Act No. 3 of 1909 and Insolvency Act No. 5 of 1990 were deleted. The said Act is a special legislation provides special procedure to be followed for declaring a person (loanee) as insolvent / bankrupt and the said .Act appears to be a remedial Act for protection of interest of the parties. Upon perusal of the said Act it appears that there is no express provisions giving retrospective effect of any existing law. As per the settled law a remedial act is not necessarily becomes retrospective unless it has been given retrospective effect by express terms or necessary intendment. There is no express term in the law giving retrospective effect of any existing law. Section 3 of the Bankruptcy Act, 1997 provides the provisions for application of the Act which runs thus:-

” ৩। এই আইন ভিন্নরূপ বিধান না থাকিলে, ইহার বিধানাবলি আপাততঃ বলবৎ অন্য কোন আইনের ক্ষুন্নকারী হইবে না, বরং অতিরিক্ত হইবে।”

13. This provision clearly expresses that the Act has not been given any retrospective effect.

14. In view of the above I am of the view that the Bankruptcy act, 1997 is not a retrospective legislation but the same is a prospective legislation.

15. Section 5 of the General Clause Act provides the procedure for coming into operation of any enactment which runs thus:-

"5 (1) Where any Act of Parliament is not expressed to come into operation on any particular day, then it shall come into operation-

(a) in the case of an Act of Parliament to which this Act was applicable before the 26th day of March, 1971, on the date on which it receives the assent; and

(b) in the case of any other Act of Parliament, the day on which the assent is first published in the official Gazette;

(2) omitted

(3) Unless the contrary is expressed, an Act of Parliament or Regulation shall be construed as coming into operation immediately on the expiration of the day preceding its commencement."

16. From section 1 sub-section (2) of Bankruptcy Act, 1997 it has seen said that the said law shall come into operation at any time after the 22nd December 1997. If section 3 of the Bankruptcy Act, 1997 is read with section 5 of the General Clauses Act it becomes clear that the Bankruptcy Act, 1997 is a prospective legislation which got no manner of application upon any pending proceeding arising out of any suit prior to the promulgation of the Act.

17. In the instant case a Title suit was instituted in the year 1989 and that was decreed. That decree was affirmed by the High Court Division with some modification and the judgment debtors were the appellant before the High Court Division who has accepted the decree. The execution proceedings No. 3 of 1990 was started long before the promulgation of Bankruptcy Act, 1997. Section 4 of the Bankruptcy Act, 1997 provides the procedure for constitution of Bankruptcy Court which runs thus:-

‘‘আদালতের গঠন, ক্ষমতা ও পদ্ধতি

৪। (১) এই আইনের অন্যান্য বিধান সাপেক্ষে, জেলা আদালত হইতে এই আইনের অধীনে এখতিয়ারসম্পন্ন আদালত এবং উক্ত আদালতের এখতিয়ারাধীণ এলাকায় এই আইনের অধীন উদ্ভুত কার্যধারাসমূহের বিচার ও নিস্পত্তিকারী বিচারক হইবেন জেলা জজ।

(২) জেলাজজ তাঁহার জজশীপে কর্মরত যেকোন অতিরিক্ত জেলাজজকে এই আইনের অধীন কার্যধারার বিচার ও নিস্পত্তি করিবার ক্ষমতা প্রদান করিতে পারেন।

(৩) উপ-ধারা (১) এবং (২) এ উল্লিখিত জজের আদালত, এই আইনের উদ্দেশ্য পূরণকল্পে দেউলিয়া বিষয়ক আদালত বলিয়া অভিহিত হইবে।”

18. After a close and careful reading to said provisions it appears that the bankruptcy Court was constituted under section 4 of the Act only for deciding suit arising out of the dispute relating to and touching the Act.

<u>19. The legislature has not given any jurisdiction to the Bankruptcy court to try any suit or execute any decree arising out of normal civil suit. So far the question of jurisdiction of the Bankruptcy court is concerned the section 38 of the Code of Civil Procedure is the guiding principle. As per section 38 of the Code of Civil Procedure the Court decreeing the suit is the Court for executing the decree unless his jurisdiction is taken away by any enactment or by any changed circumstances. As per section 38 of the Code of Civil Procedure and as per general rule the territorial jurisdiction is a condition precedent to a Court executing a decree and no Court can execute a decree with respect to property situated entirely outside its jurisdiction. That view finds support from the case law of Mathai -v- Varkey, AIR 1964 (SC) 907.</u>

20. In view of the above I find that the Bankruptcy Court at Dhaka has got no jurisdiction to execute the decree. It is the settled law that the executing Court cannot go beyond the decree and the said Court is bound to execute the decree as it stands. The executing Court cannot transfer any execution proceeding from his Court to any other Court unless his jurisdiction is taken away. The transfer of an execution proceeding is guided by section 39 of the Code of Civil Procedure. As per the said provision the Court can transfer a proceedings only upon receipt of an application from the decree holder but not at the desire of the judgment debtors. In the instant case the execution case being No. 3 of 1990 was started on 24.10.1990.The auction sale was made lawfully. The sale was confirmed duly and sale certificate was issued and thereafter the same was registered as per law are the admitted facts. From the facts and circumstances and the discussions as made above I am constrained to hold-

(a) section 33(1) of the Act and the Act 1997 itself has got no manner of application in a pending execution case arising out of a civil court's decree to execute a decree prior to the promulgation of the said Act.

(b) The Bankruptcy court constituted under Act 1997 has got no jurisdiction to execute the Execution case No. 3 of 1990 pending before the Joint District Judge, 1st court, Naogoan.

21. In view of the admitted facts it appears that the Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Naogoan being the execution court has executed the part of the decree on full satisfaction as per order 21 Rule-94 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Now the rest part is yet to be executed under Order 21 rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure which runs thus:-

"95. Where the immovable property sold is in the occupancy of the judgment-debtor or of some person on his behalf or of some person claiming under a title created by the judgment-debtor subsequently to the attachment of such property and a certificate in respect thereof has been granted under rule 94, the Court shall, on the application of the purchaser, order delivery to be made by putting such purchaser or any person whom he may appoint to receive delivery on his behalf in possession of the property, and, if need be, by removing any person who refuses to vacate the same."

22. After perusal of the said provisions it appears that the Joint District Judge, 1st court, Noagaon being the executing Court is bound to hand over delivery of possession through process of Court and with the help of police forces and he got no other alternative but to execute the decree as per order 21 Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The said executing Court at the last stage of the execution proceeding has deliberately fallen into an error of law and allowed application under section 33(1) of the Bankruptcy Act, 1997 although that provision got no manner of application in any execution case which has been started before the promulgation of the Act, 1997. The learned Additional District Judge also being the revisional Court has totally failed to assume the jurisdiction of an executing Court as provided under section 38 of the Code of Civil Procedure and has failed to understand the purpose of promulgation of Bankruptcy Act, 1997 as well as its application. Both the Courts below have committed an error of law resulting an error in the decision occasioning a failure of justice in allowing application under section 33(1) of the Bankruptcy Act, 1997 in a proceeding which has been started long before the promulgation of the Act, 1997.

23. From the facts and circumstances and discussions made above I find substance in the leave granting order. Both the Courts below have erred in law in entertaining the application under section 33(1) of the Bankruptcy Act, 1997 in a pending execution case arising out of a decree passed in a suit instituted and decreed prior to the promulgation of the Act, 1997. Accordingly the leave granting order is made absolute and the impugned judgment and order dated 10/9/2006 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Naogaon in Civil Revision No. 62 of 2005 dismissing the Civil Revision and affirming the order dated 25.9.2005 passed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Naogaon in Execution Case No. 3 of 1990 are set aside. The application under section 33(1) of the Bankruptcy Act, 1997 filed in the said Execution Case is rejected. The executing Court is directed to hand over possession of the auction purchased land in favour of the decree holder petitioners through police forces and through the Nazir of the Court within 30(thirty) days from the date of receipt of this order without fail. The said Court is further directed to communicate the compliance of this order within 60(sixty) days to this court. The order of stay granted by this Court earlier stands vacated.

24. The office is directed to send down the lower Court's record at once. Let a copy of the judgment be transmitted to the courts concerned at their respective station.

End.

full_judgment:
Afzal Hossain Ahmed, J:This Rule, at the instance of the plaintiff-respondent-petitioners, was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 19.9.2004 ( decree signed on 29.9.2004 ) passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Kushtia in T. A. No. 143 of 2001 reversing the judgment and decree dated 16.9.2001 and (decree signed 'on 23.9.2001) passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Mirpur in T.S. No. 14 of 1998 dismissing the suit should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Facts necessary for disposal of this revisional application, briefly, be put thus:-

The plaintiff-respondent-petitioners, as plaintiffs, instituted Title Suit being No. 14 of 1998 for declaration of title and also for declaration that the Heba-bil-ewaz deeds being Nos. 4080 of 1997 and 4266 of 1997 are fraudulent, forged, collusive, and not binding upon the plaintiffs.

3. Plaintiff Nos. 1-5 are full brothers, and the sole defendant is ark sister and the plain-tiff No.6 is their mother. The aforesaid two registered deeds are Heba-biদ-ewaz deeds in respect of the suit land mentioned in the schedule to the plaint which were executed by one Lokman Sander in favour of his daughter, Mst. Amena Khatun which are under challenge. 

4. During trial defendant No.5 Abdul Jalil compromised the case with the defendant and the rest plaintiffs contested the case. 

5. The sole defendant Mst. Amena Khatun contested the suit by filing a written statement denying all the material allegations as made in the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the suit land mentioned in the schedule to the plaint belonged to her father, Lokman Sander who transferred the same to his only daughter, the defendant No.1 by executing registered Heba-bil-ewaz deeds No.4080 and 4266 dated 8.6.1997 and 15.6.1997 respectively and delivering possession thereof to the defendant No. 1. Lokman Hossain Sarder also transferred his other lands in favour of the plaintiff Nos. 1-5 by different deeds. The defendant No.1 after getting the suit land through the aforesaid Heba-bil-ewaz deeds got the suit jams mutated in her name vide Mutation Case No. 298/9-2/97-98 and 299/9-2/97-98 and since then has been possessing the suit land by paying rent to the Government. It is further contended that the plaintiffs without having any right title and interest in the suit land filed the suit on false allegations and with ulterior motive with intent to grab the suit land. 

6. During trial 4 witnesses for the plaintiffs and 8 for the defendant were examined in the suit and both the parties also adduced documentary evidence in support of their respective cases. 

7. The learned Assistant Judge, Mirpur, Kushtia considering all the evidence adduced by the parties decreed the suit against the defendant No.1 as prayed for by the plaintiffs. 

8. Being aggrieved by that judgment and decree dated 16.9.2001 the defendant preferred appeal being Title Appeal No. 143 of 2001. Ultimately, the learned Additional District Judge, First Court, Kushtia, allowed the appeal setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court on 16.9.2001 in T.S. No. 14/1998 and dismissing the Suit against which three, out of the 6 plaintiff-respondents have preferred this revisional application and obtained the present Rule. 

9. Mr. Shasti Sarker, assisted by Mr. Khandaker Nozrul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that Lokman Sarder, father of the plaintiffs 1-5 and defendant No.1 never executed the Heba-bil-ewaz deeds under challenge in respect of the suit land in favour of the defendant No.1 and that the said deeds are fraudulent, forged, collusive, ultra vires and not binding upon the plaintiffs. The trial Court considering the evidence, both oral and documentary, adduced by the plaintiffs had rightly decreed the suit against the defendant and the appellate Court below without appreciating the evidence adduced by the plaintiffs most illegally allowed the appeal dismissing the suit and thereby committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and as such the same is not sustainable in law. 

10. Mr. Md. Nurul Amin, assisted by Mr. Md. Amimul Ehsan, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No.1 submits that the suit land belonged to one Lokman Sarder who transferred the same in favour of his only daughter, the defendant Amena Khatun by executing two registered Heba-bil-ewaz deeds as above and since then she has been possessing the suit land by mutating the jama in her name and paying rent to the Government and the said Heba-bil-ewaz deeds have duly been acted upon. Mr. Amin has further submitted that the plaintiffs without having any right, title, interest and possession in the suit land filed the suit suppressing the fact and challenging the aforesaid Heba-bil-ewaz deeds only with intent to grab the suit land and that the P.Ws. 2,3 and 4 have stated corroborating each other that both the plaintiffs and defendant possess the suit land jointly. If that be so, the plaintiffs should have sought for declaration of their title to the suit land specifying their own shares therein as required under Order VII Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure but that has not been done in the instant case and in view of that without a suit for declaration of title and for joint possession or recovery of khas possession or partition Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is not available to attract the relief sought for in the instant suit. Mr. Amin has further submitted that the trial Court as well as the appellate Court below did not at all consider the aforesaid pertinent aspects of the matter although the appellate Court, ultimately, allowed the appeal on other aspects of the matter in consideration of the evidence available on record and as such there is no reason to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court below. 

11. Heard the learned Advocates of both the sides and perused the impugned judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court as well as those passed by the trial Court, the oral and documentary evidence adduced by the parties and the other materials available on records. 

12. The point for determination in this Rule is whether the impugned judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court below dated 19.9.2004 setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the Assistant Judge, Mirpur, Kushtia in Title Suit No. 14 of 1998 dismissing the suit is sustainable in law. 

13. Plaintiffs have instituted the Suit being No. 14 of 1998 for declaration of their title to the suit land and also for declaration that the Heba-bil-ewaz deeds No. 4080 and 4266 of 1997 are fraudulent, forged, collusive, ultra vires and not binding upon them. Thus, the plaintiffs have claimed their exclusive title to the suit land explicitly disowning the title of the defendant No.1, Mst. Amena Khatun. But it appears from the testimony of P.Ws. 2,3 and 4 that they have categorically said by corroborating each other that both the plaintiffs and the defendant possess the suit land. If that be so, the plaintiffs should have sought for declaration of their title to the suit land with joint possession or should have prayed for recovery of khas possession or partition but no such relief has been sought for in the instant suit. Moreso, the portion of the suit land in which the plaintiffs are in possession have not been specified as required under Order VII, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Without having prayed for such relief a simple suit for declaration of title to the suit land, as precisely has been done in the instant suit, is not at all maintainable and without seeking for such relief Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is not available to attract the relief sought for in the instant suit. It appears that with a view to arrive at a correct decision in the instant case the above pertinent aspects of the matter should have been taken into consideration by the trial Court but of no avail. It appears that the lower appellate Court was also inadvertent to settle the said pertinent aspects of the matter.

14. Further it appears that the Plaintiff No.5 Abdul Jalil, during trial, compromised the suit with the defendant No.1 Mst. Amena Khatun admitting her claim in respect of the suit land.

15. Plaintiff No.6 is the mother of the plaintiffs 1-5 and the defendant No.1 Mst. Amena Khatun and as such she was the best and most reliable witness in the case to testify the veracity of the plaintiffs' claim but mysteriously she has not been examined in this case. Withholding of such an important witness gives rise to presumption that had she been examined she would not have supported the plaintiffs' claim which looked askance at the veracity of the claim of the plaintiffs. It appears that both the Courts below were inadvertent to take this important aspect of the matter into consideration. 

16. The plaintiffs have filed the suit alleging that the Heba-bil-ewaz deeds under challenge are forged, fraudulent, collusive and created by false personification. Had it been so, it was the onus on the plaintiffs to prove sending the Heba-bil-ewaz deeds under challenge to the Hand Writing Experts to compare with the deeds executed by Lokman Sarder in their favour or other admitted deeds with a view to ascertain whether the said Heba-bil-ewaz deeds were at all executed by Lokman Sarder. Defendant has categorically stated in her written statement that her father, Lokman Sarder had given his other lands to the Plaintiff Nos. 1-5 by executing deeds, the Certified copies of which have been marked as Exts. Chha- Uma. But the plaintiffs did neither deny the execution of such deeds nor discharge such onus on them even though the opportunity to discharge such onus was open to them.

17. There is a presumption of good faith in human transaction and who alleges bad faith such as fraud needs to prove the same. In the instant case, the plaintiffs were pleading that it was a case of fraud and as such they need to prove the same. Further, it was the plaintiffs, who wish the Court to believe in the existence or non-existence of a material fact. It was, thus, for the plaintiffs to prove the non-existence of that material fact, namely, the non-existence of the Heba-bil-ewaz deeds in question in the eye of law and, further if no evidence was led on either side it would be the plaintiffs who would lose. Therefore, on all counts, it was for the plaintiffs to prove the fraudulent character of the deed and this they cannot prove by the weakness, if any, in defence testimony. 

18. Admittedly, the Heba-bil-ewaz deeds in question are registered deeds. It is true that registration of a document would prove its registration and due execution only and not the truth or otherwise of the contents or the recitals appearing in the document. Those need to be proved if challenged to be incorrect both as to title and as to delivery of possession. Though registration itself would not conclusively prove the truth of the contents of a documents yet the recitals in a document, admitted by the executants before the Registrar would create a rebuttable presumption as to correctness of the facts stated therein and the onus would lie upon the party alleging otherwise as there exists a general presumption of good faith and legality in all human transactions. 

19. Since the plaintiffs allege the fraudulent character of the Heba-bil-ewaz deeds in question and also allege otherwise as there exists a general presumption of good faith and legality in all human transactions the onus to prove such allegations would lie upon the plaintiffs. But I find from the evidence available on record that although the plaintiffs examined as many as 4 witnesses in the instant case they could not succeed in substantiating the fraudulent character of the heba-bil-ewaz deeds in question as well as the presumption against good faith and legality in all human transactions and, thus, the plaintiffs have hopelessly failed to discharge the onus on them. 

20. Besides, the defendant claimed that after getting the suit land from her father through the Heba-bil-ewaz deeds in question she got the suit jama mutated in her name and has been possessing the same since then and in support of this contention she has filed D.C.R., Khariji khatian and rent receipts marked Exts. Ghha-Uma and Cha. The said papers as exhibited by the defendant are important items of evidence of possession which may be used as collateral evidence of title since generally possession follows title which in respect of the suit land prima facie stands in favour of the defendant. In spite of the fact if the plaintiffs claim exclusive title to the suit land, they should have prayed for confirmation of possession but that having not been done the maintainability of the suit is called in question. Besides, D.Ws. 4 and 5 identifier and witness respectively of the disputed deeds have proved the execution of the deeds by the donor. D.W.6 was present when the said Heba-bil-ewaz deeds were executed by the donor. Moreso, D.Ws. 2 and 3 have deposed corroborating each other that the defendant has been in possession of the suit land. 

21. It is contended from the side of the petitioners that consideration of the deeds i.e. "Tasbi and Jainamaj" were not at all given to its donor. With a view to rebut this the learned Advocate for the opposite party No.1 has submitted that the plaintiffs not being the donors of the Heba-bil-ewaz deeds in question, they are not competent to question whether the consideration passed or not and that only the donor is competent to claim the same. In support of his submission the learned Advoate for the opposite party No. 1 has cited a decision in the Case of Guru Charan Mondal and others Vs. Sree Bhaba Sindhu Sarkar and others reported in 1 EX File Plus (AD) 73 which I find compatible with his above submission. 

22. Considering all the above aspects of the matter I am inclined to hold that the trial Court in coming to the decision decreeing the suit against the defendant did not properly appreciate the evidence both oral and documentary adduced by the parties and also did not address the pertinent questions of law involved in the case as referred to above and as such the same is not sustainable in law. 

23. In view of the above I find that the learned appellate Court below in appreciation of the evidence on record adduced by the parties has rightly taken the view in coming to the decision allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court although some pertinent questions of law involved in the case, as I have discussed above, were not properly addressed. However, considering all the aspects of the matter I find no reason to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree dated 19.9.2004 as there having no merit in this Rule. 

24. In the result, the Rule is discharged, however, without any order as to costs. 

25. Send down the Lower Court Records at once. 

End.
